Typography vocabulary

Short definitions and examples for the terms you meet while exploring fonts.

43 terms across 6 topics

Families and faces

Compare regular and bold
Typography

The practice of choosing and arranging type so people can read and understand text.

Example Choosing a heading face and spacing a paragraph are both typography.

Typeface

A design for a set of letters and other characters.

Example Lora is a typeface design.

Font family

A group of related font styles that share a design.

Example A family can include regular, bold, and italic faces.

Font face

One specific style within a family.

Example Lora Bold Italic is a face; Lora is the family.

Font

A resource that supplies letter shapes and layout information. People also use this word loosely for a face or family.

Example A web font file lets a browser display a particular design.

Glyph

A drawn form used to represent a character or a combination of characters.

Example A font can offer more than one drawn form for the same letter.

Weight

How heavy or light the strokes of a face are.

Example Regular often uses 400 and bold often uses 700; available weights vary.

Italic

A style with slanted letterforms that may have different shapes from the upright design.

Example An italic a can have a different construction from an upright a.

Oblique

A slanted style that usually keeps the construction of the upright letters.

Example Slant alone does not necessarily make a design a true italic.

Font types

Compare serif fonts
Serif

A small finishing stroke attached to a main stroke; also the category of typefaces with these features.

Example Look at the ends of the stems in a capital H.

Sans serif

A typeface without serifs.

Example Sans means without; the letter endings have no added serifs.

Display

Type designed primarily for larger, attention-getting settings.

Example A display face may suit a headline but be difficult to read in a small paragraph.

Handwriting

Type that suggests letters made by hand.

Example Some faces resemble casual handwriting; others resemble formal calligraphy.

Script

Type inspired by written or calligraphic forms, often with connected strokes.

Example Script is a more specific idea than the broad handwriting label.

Monospace

Type in which every character is allotted the same horizontal space.

Example Compare iiiii and WWWWW: both strings have the same advance width.

Proportional

Type with character widths that vary.

Example A narrow i usually takes less horizontal space than a W.

Letter anatomy

Inspect letter shapes
Baseline

The reference line that letters sit on.

Example Parts of g, p, and y can extend below it.

X-height

The height of a lowercase x measured from the baseline.

Example Two fonts at the same size can have visibly different lowercase heights.

Cap height

The height of flat-topped capital letters above the baseline.

Example Compare a capital H with a lowercase x.

Ascender

The part of a lowercase letter that rises above the x-height.

Example The tall part of b, d, or h is an ascender.

Descender

The part of a letter that extends below the baseline.

Example Look at the lower strokes in p, q, and y.

Counter

The space inside or partly surrounded by a letterform.

Example Look inside o, p, and e.

Aperture

The opening into a partly enclosed letter shape.

Example Compare how open a c or e appears.

Stem

A main upright or diagonal stroke in a letter.

Example The vertical strokes of H are stems.

Bowl

A rounded stroke that encloses a counter.

Example The curved part of a b is its bowl.

Terminal

The end of a stroke that is not a serif.

Example Notice the stroke endings in a, c, and f.

Stroke contrast

The difference in thickness between strokes within the letterforms.

Example Compare the thin and thick parts of a serif O.

Spacing and size

Try letter spacing
Font size

The size of the design’s em square, rather than the exact height of a visible letter.

Example A 36px font does not guarantee a capital letter that is 36px tall.

Kerning

An adjustment to the space between particular pairs of characters.

Example AV may need a different spacing adjustment from HH.

Tracking / letter spacing

Spacing added across a run of text.

Example Changing letter spacing affects the whole sentence, rather than just a selected pair.

Line height

The height used for each line box in CSS; it controls the spacing of successive lines.

Example At a font size of 20px, a unitless line height of 1.5 gives a 30px line box.

Leading

The traditional spacing of lines of type, often discussed as the distance between baselines. In CSS, extra space is distributed around the text within the line box.

Example The line-height control is the practical way to explore vertical text spacing here.

Em

A relative unit based on font size; the reference depends on the CSS property.

Example For letter-spacing at a 20px font size, 0.1em adds 2px.

Measure / line length

The horizontal length of a line of text.

Example Narrow a paragraph and it wraps into more lines.

Reading and layout

Compare confusing characters
Legibility

How easily you can distinguish individual characters.

Example Can you tell a capital I, a lowercase l, and the digit 1 apart?

Readability

How comfortably someone can read a passage of text in context.

Example A readable paragraph depends on type, size, spacing, contrast, and line length.

Hierarchy

Differences in emphasis that show which information to read first.

Example A larger heading and a quieter caption have different jobs.

Alignment

How lines of text line up within their available space.

Example Left-aligned text shares a left edge; centered text balances around the middle.

Variable fonts and coverage

Explore available font faces
Variable font

A font that can provide a range of styles through adjustable design axes.

Example One font may allow continuous changes in weight rather than separate files for each weight.

Axis

An adjustable dimension in a variable font, with a defined range.

Example wght adjusts weight, wdth adjusts width, and opsz adjusts optical size when supported.

Optical size

Design adjustments intended for different reading sizes.

Example Small text may need sturdier details than a large headline; availability depends on the font.

Subset

A selection of characters within a font’s coverage.

Example The catalogue may list Latin, Greek, or Cyrillic subsets.

Fallback font

A backup font used when the preferred font cannot supply the needed text.

Example A page may temporarily use a fallback while its web font loads.
